guides.title: Wallacea to Sahul: Early Hominins, Sea Crossings & Deep-Time Pioneers
guides.description: A million years of strait crossings across Flores, Sulawesi, Timor, Alor, and Raja Ampat leading into Pleistocene Sahul.
guides.intro: Even at glacial low sea stands, deep oceanic trenches separated Southeast Asia (Sunda) from Australia and New Guinea (Sahul). Yet hominins reached Flores over one million years ago and Homo sapiens sailed east to Raja Ampat and Arnhem Land before 50,000 years ago.
guides.scope: Archaic Wallacean hominins (Wolo Sege, Mata Menge, Liang Bua), Sulawesi karst art, pelagic fisheries in Timor and Alor, Denisovan genomic admixture, and the Northern Route gateway at Mololo Cave.

map.scope: Basin and karst cave localities bridging Wallacea and northern Sahul; coastlines show modern sea levels rather than exposed Pleistocene continental shelves.

points.label: Wolo Sege & Mata Menge (Flores)
points.description: Stone tools at Wolo Sege and miniature early Middle Pleistocene mandibles/humerus at Mata Menge reveal diminutive hominins settled Flores well before Homo sapiens.

points.label: Liang Bua Cave (Flores)
points.description: Limestone cavern yielding Homo floresiensis skeletons (~100–60 ka) and stone industries ending around a 61 ka regional drying pulse.

points.label: Walanae Basin & Maros Karst (Sulawesi)
points.description: Early Pleistocene river-terrace artifacts (>1 Ma) plus the world's oldest dated cave hand stencils and figurative scenes in Maros–Pangkep karsts.

points.label: Asitau Kuru (Timor) & Tron Bon Lei (Alor)
points.description: Deep maritime caves documenting ~44 ka pelagic tuna capture, rotating shell fishhooks, and Pleistocene obsidian transfers among Lesser Sunda islands.

points.label: Mololo Cave (Waigeo, Raja Ampat)
points.description: Equatorial karst shelter recording the earliest radiocarbon-dated human plant-resin processing and foraging along the Northern Route into Sahul.

sections.heading: Archaic island hominins across Wallace's Line

paragraphs.text: Archaeological horizons in the So'a Basin of Flores (Wolo Sege, 1.02 Ma) and Sulawesi's Walanae Valley prove that early hominins repeatedly crossed open deep-water channels without terrestrial bridges. By 700,000 years ago at Mata Menge, isolated selective pressures had already produced tiny hominins ancestral to Homo floresiensis.

Revised stratigraphy at Liang Bua shows that Homo floresiensis disappeared shortly after 60–50 ka amid monsoon aridification—right around the window when modern human voyagers and ancient Denisovan-introgressed lineages crossed Wallacea toward Sahul.

Agent-based drift and least-cost voyaging models show both a Northern Route (Kalimantan → Sulawesi → Moluccas → Bird's Head New Guinea) and a Southern Route (Bali → Flores → Timor → NW Australia Shelf), substantiated directly by 55–50 ka tree-resin finds at Mololo Cave and 67.8–44 ka sites in Sulawesi, Timor, and Alor.

guides.title: Pleistocene Australia: Madjedbebe, Kimberley Shelters, Willandra & Arid Pioneers
guides.description: First Nations settlement across tropical Arnhem Land, Kimberley coastlands, Flinders Ranges, and the Murray–Darling lakes from 65,000 years ago onward.
guides.intro: Within millennia of Sahul landfall, Aboriginal families adapted across every Australian biome—from Kakadu escarpments and shelf islands in the northwest to freezing glacial claypans along Lake Mungo, the Nullarbor subterranean karsts, and Blue Mountains ridge camps.
guides.scope: Key Australian Pleistocene stratigraphic, fossil, rock-art, and paleoecological localities before 10,000 BCE.

map.scope: Key Pleistocene sites across continental Australia; Barrow Island and Arnhem/Kimberley plains once overlooked wide exposed shelves.

points.description: Ground-edge stone hatchets, hematite processing, Pandanus nutshells, and continuous 65 ka seed-grinding stones.

points.label: Boodie Cave & Kimberley Shelters (WA)
points.description: Pleistocene marine shelf shells, ochre-dusted necklaces, and 16–12 ka mud-wasp-dated Gwion rock paintings in NW Australia.

points.description: Australia's oldest arid-zone sequence (49 ka gypsum-ash strata) paired with LGM deep subterranean flint mines on the Nullarbor Plain.

points.description: WLH 1 cremation, WLH 3 ochre burial, >450 fossilized human footprints (~20 ka), and terminal Pleistocene cemeteries across the Murray–Willandra system.

points.label: Dargan Shelter, Parramatta & Cloggs Cave (SE Australia)
points.description: Pre-LGM alluvial ochre workshops, 20 ka Blue Mountains high-elevation habitation (1,073 m), and 25 ka Gunaikurnai Gippsland deposits.

points.label: Cuddie Springs Claypan (NSW)
points.description: Ephemeral wetland preserving Diprotodon bones alongside grinding stones, central to debates over human-megafauna overlap vs taphonomic reworking.

paragraphs.text: Genomic analyses of Aboriginal Australian diversity harmonize with deep OSL dates at Madjedbebe, coastal Barrow Island, and Kimberley rock shelters to support Sahul colonization before 50–65 ka. From the start, inhabitants processed Pandanus nuts, ground silica-rich grass seeds, shaped edge-ground axes, and processed mineral pigments.

During the Last Glacial Maximum (~24–18 ka), families adapted simultaneously to hyper-arid dunes around Willandra (leaving claypan footprints), pitch-black Nullarbor flint shafts (Koonalda), and snow-dusted Blue Mountains overhangs (Dargan Shelter).

sections.heading: Arid-zone resilience, nullarbor flint & coastal shelves

paragraphs.text: Long before postglacial seas rose, Aboriginal people harvested marine shellfish along Barrow Island (50 ka), mined subterranean chalky flint deep inside Koonalda Cave on the Nullarbor Plain, and painted mud-wasp-dated Gwion and Wandjina panels across the Kimberley.

Archaeological research continues to refine single-grain OSL sand chronologies at Madjedbebe and Nauwalabila I while testing whether Pleistocene sites like Cuddie Springs reflect genuine megafauna hunting or claypan taphonomic reworking.

guides.title: Lutruwita / Tasmania: Ice-Age Caves, Bass Strait Separation & Aboriginal Survival
guides.description: 41,600 years of fire ecology, glacial Southwest karst hunting, kelp-vessel engineering, resistance in the Black War, and survival.
guides.intro: Across the exposed Bassian land bridge before 41,600 years ago, Palawa ancestors entered Lutruwita—the southernmost ice-age frontier on Earth—before sea-level rise severed Bass Strait ~14–10 ka ago.
guides.scope: Landscape fire cores, Southwest karst refugia (Kutikina, Warreen, Nunamira), eastern Holocene sites, kelp *rikawa* water craft, and 1824–1847 colonial war and exile.

sections.heading: From glacial karst hunters to island resilience

paragraphs.text: By 41,600 years ago Aboriginal cultural burning cleared closed temperate rainforest tracts across northern Lutruwita. As ice-age winds intensified, families sheltered inside Southwest limestone caverns—Kutikina, Warreen, Nunamira—specializing in Bennett's wallaby marrow extraction and transporting impactite Darwin glass across icy river valleys.

Rising Bass Strait waters severed Tasmania around 14–10 ka. Palawa communities flourished along open eastern plains and offshore Hunter/Fleurieu islands, crafting bark canoes and bull-kelp *rikawa* water vessels prior to the 1824–1832 Black War and survival beyond colonial containment.

cells: Peat/lake charcoal shift in NW Tasmania
Guerrilla defense, Black Line & Wybalenna persistence

paragraphs.text: Following Bass Strait's flooding ~14–10 ka, eastern Lutruwita communities sustained open grassy woodlands via selective firing while fabricating sturdy bark canoes and thick bull-kelp *rikawa* water containers to forage outer Hunter and Fleurieu islands.

From 1824–1832 Palawa bands mounted coordinated resistance against settler pastoral intrusion across the Midlands, surviving the 1830 Black Line and Flinders Island exile (Wybalenna) to assert continuing heritage.

guides.title: Continental Trade Routes of Aboriginal Australia: Ochre, Pituri, Greenstone & Pearl Shell
guides.description: Transcontinental kinship exchange highways carrying red ochre, narcotic pituri, Kulin greenstone hatchets, Kimberley pearl shell, and Arnhem–Makassar trade.
guides.intro: Far from isolated bands, Aboriginal Australia was crisscrossed by thousands of kilometres of ceremonial Songline trade corridors moving prized ochres, stone blades, baler shells, and narcotics across arid deserts and river basins.
guides.scope: Geochemically sourced ochre (Wilgie Mia, Parachilna), Mulligan *pituri*, Mount William greenstone axes, Kimberley *riji* shell, Torres Strait, and Macassan maritime trade.

sections.heading: Sourced materials across desert & river networks

paragraphs.text: Scientific provenance methods (LA-ICP-MS, portable XRF, XRD, and direct AMS radiocarbon on shells and wooden artifacts) now trace Aboriginal Australian exchange objects far beyond 19th-century ethnographic maps. Shimmering specular ochre from Wilgie Mia (WA) and Pukardu (SA) moved along structured Dreaming tracks carrying pituri (*Duboisia*) south from the Georgina–Mulligan basin.

Across southeastern waterways, greenstone blanks from Mount William (*Wil-im-ee Moor-ring*) traveled >700 km along Murray–Darling kinship ties, mirrored in Northern Australia's *leilira* blades and maritime exchange across Torres Strait and Arnhem Land's trepang coasts.

sections.heading: Kimberley pearl shell, desert balers & sandstone grindstones

paragraphs.text: Directly radiocarbon-dated marine baler shells (*Melo*) and incised *riji* pearl-shell pendants found over 1,500 km inland across the Great Sandy and Gibson Deserts demonstrate continental social webs tying northwestern reef harvesters to Central Australian groups.

sections.heading: Arnhem Land–Makassar *trepang* fleets & Torres Strait mariners

paragraphs.text: Across Australia's northern seas, Yolŋu communities harvested sea cucumbers alongside monsoon fleets from Makassar (leaving rock-art paintings, tamarinds, and loanwords), while Torres Strait islanders mediated Papuan outriggers with Cape York ochre.

guides.title: Conflict & Resistance in Australia: From Pre-Colonial Evidence to the Frontier Wars
guides.description: Bioarchaeological conflict trauma along the Darling River paired with 1794–1900 archaeological and historical records of Frontier Wars resistance.
guides.intro: Archaeology and historical forensics reveal both deeply rooted pre-colonial conflict regulation (and lethal weapon trauma like Kaakutja on the Baaka–Darling River) and a century-long guerrilla defense across colonial pastoral and policing frontiers.

sections.heading: Material traces of pre-colonial conflict & asymmetrical frontier war

paragraphs.text: Despite older generalizations about the 'archaeological invisibility' of Australian warfare, close osteology (e.g., Kaakutja on the Baaka–Darling and Roonka on the Murray) alongside shield and spear depictions confirm regulated pre-colonial violence.

Between 1788 and 1900, British settlers, militias, and Native Mounted Police detachments faced agile Indigenous guerrilla resistance—from Hawkesbury sandstone ridges and Tasmania's Midlands to Kooroongoora Warrior Lodges and Kimberley limestone caves—reconstructed via ballistic artifact surveys and conflict rock art.

sections.heading: Regional resistance from Hawkesbury & Pinjarra to Windjana Gorge

paragraphs.text: Organized Indigenous tactics evolved rapidly across terrains—ranging from Darug corn-raid guerrilla strategy along the Hawkesbury (1794–1816) and Kalkadoon defense in NW Queensland crags (1884) to Bunuba leader Jandamarra's Kimberley gorge campaign (1894–1897).

sections.heading: Archival silence, Native Mounted Police & landscape forensics

paragraphs.text: Systematic archaeological surveys of Queensland Native Mounted Police detachments, cartridge spreads, and oral histories across Overland Corner and Dead Man's Flat recover conflict events systematically omitted from colonial ledgers.

guides.title: New Guinea & Papua: Highland Agriculture, Bird's Head Pioneers, Hiri & the Kula Ring
guides.description: From 50 ka montane forests and Kuk Swamp wetland drainage to coastal Hiri pottery fleets and Massim *Kula* exchange.
guides.intro: Joined to Australia throughout most of the Ice Age as northern Sahul, New Guinea became an independent center of highland agriculture and later anchored some of the Pacific's largest maritime exchange rings.
guides.scope: Ivane Valley, Kuk Swamp, Walufeni/Simbai Highlands, Lachitu, Auwim East Sepik, Caution Bay/Motupore Hiri, and Massim Kula ring.

points.description: Independent highland ditch agriculture by 4,500 BP, Walufeni shell imports, and highland-coast pottery contact.

paragraphs.text: In the Wahgi Valley (Kuk Swamp) and Southern Highlands, Papuan societies independently cleared montane forests, hunted, and dug drainage ditches by 4,500 BP while exchanging marine shells far inland over misty passes.

Along coastal New Guinea, Lapita mariners reached Caution Bay and Giligilina ~2,900 BP before local specialization generated three legendary maritime systems: the Hiri *lagatoi* sago-pottery trade in the Papuan Gulf, Bel–Siassi Voyagers across Vitiaz Strait, and the Massim *Kula* Ring.

paragraphs.text: Rock-art shelters at Auwim along the Upper Karawari River and interior caves such as Walufeni preserve marine shell wealth and shared highland pottery motifs connecting remote mountain ridges to coastal estuaries.

From Caution Bay and Emo along southern Papua to Milne Bay island ossuaries, ceramic sourcing and genome-wide surveys trace centuries of evolving maritime kinship underpinning the Hiri and Kula networks.

guides.title: Island Melanesia & Lapita: Obsidian Corridors, Villages & Chiefdoms
guides.description: Pleistocene crossings across the Bismarcks and Solomons, ~1200 BCE Lapita expansion to Vanuatu and New Caledonia, and Roviana war-canoe hillforts.
guides.intro: Inhabitants of New Ireland and Manus crossed open waters 45,000–21,000 years ago; millennia later, Lapita outrigger fleets fused local obsidian networks with Austronesian pottery to reach Vanuatu and New Caledonia in a historical blink.
guides.scope: Bismarcks (Talasea, Watom, Lou, Anir), Kilu/Solomons (Roviana hillforts), Teouma (Vanuatu), and Koné (New Caledonia).

map.scope: Major obsidian quarries, Lapita villages, cemeteries, and fortified lagoons across Island Melanesia.

points.label: Talasea, Makekur & Watom (New Britain)
points.description: Volcanic glass quarry and early Lapita stilt villages anchoring Near Oceania long-distance canoe voyages.

points.label: Lou (Manus) & Anir (New Ireland)
points.description: Admiralty Islands obsidian that displaced New Britain sources across late Lapita and post-Lapita reefs.

points.label: Nusa Roviana & New Georgia (Solomon Islands)
points.description: Fortified coral hillforts, coastal *hope* shrines, and shell-ring economics fueling *tomoko* headhunting networks.

points.description: Pioneering Remote Oceania necropolis preserving Talasea obsidian, Lapita cylinder urns, and genomic admixture transitions.

points.description: Name-site Lapita settlement importing Bismarck volcanic glass prior to complex Kanak irrigated terraces.

paragraphs.text: Pleistocene explorers first carried Talasea and Lou obsidian between New Ireland and Manus more than 20,000 years ago. From ~1200–1000 BCE, Lapita canoes pushed these standardized volcanic-glass blades over 3,000 km southeast into Vanuatu (Teouma), New Caledonia (Koné), and Fiji.

Subsequent genetic and archaeological turnovers in Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands generated culturally rich, defended Melanesian polities—exemplified by Roviana Lagoon coral hillforts and long-distance war-canoe networks.

cells: Founding cemetery, dentate pottery & ancient DNA

sections.heading: Bismarck origins: from 40 ka reefs to Makekur & Watom

paragraphs.text: Deep limestone caves on New Ireland and Manus establish over 40,000 years of open-water adaptation before Lapita stilt villages crystallized at Makekur (Arawe) and Watom Island around 3,300–2,700 BP.

Genetic sampling at Teouma combined with chemical pottery sourcing charts rapid post-Lapita Papuan admixture across Vanuatu, culminating millennia later in fortified New Georgia lagoons and *tomoko* war-canoe chiefdoms in the Solomons.

guides.title: Micronesia’s Stone & Coral Worlds: Marianas Latte, Palau, Yap, Nan Madol & Leluh
guides.description: Direct 1500 BCE open-ocean colonization followed by carved volcanic Palau hills, Yap *rai* stone money, Pohnpei basalt islets, and Kosrae coral pyramids.
guides.intro: Separated by vast sweeps of the tropical northwest Pacific, Micronesian navigators pioneered independent 2,000-km crossings by 1500 BCE and later raised some of the Pacific's boldest megalithic civic landscapes.
guides.scope: Marianas *latte* villages, Palau Babeldaob terraces, Yap *rai* quarries and *sawei* canoe tributes, Pohnpei Nan Madol, and Kosrae Leluh.

sections.heading: Engineering stone & ledger networks across Oceania

paragraphs.text: By ~1500 BCE, early Chamorro ancestors sailed >2,000 km east across open Pacific swells into the Marianas, later developing ranked *Latte* stone architecture and taro systems.

Further south across Micronesia, societies reshaped entire volcanic landscapes into Babeldaob terraced hilltops, operated a multi-atoll ledger monetary system linking Palau and Yap via monumental *rai* stone disks, and built Nan Madol and Leluh as coral-basalt hydraulic capitals.

Excavations inside Omis Cave in Palau and village ceremonial grounds on Yap illuminate how massive limestone disks (*rai*) anchored hierarchical exchange and relational accounting across hundreds of kilometres of open Carolinian atolls.

sections.heading: Basalt canals at Nan Madol & Leluh coral tombs

paragraphs.text: Trace-element XRF sourcing on Pohnpei alongside U-series coral dates at Kosrae reveal coordinated island states engineering monumental basalt-log sanctuaries, agroforestry seawalls, and coastal pyramidal tombs between 1100 and 1600 CE.

guides.intro: Around the International Date Line, Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, and Futuna formed the crucible where Remote Oceanic Lapita voyagers transformed into classic Polynesian maritime chiefdoms.
guides.scope: Bourewa, Vatia & Bua Fijian hillforts, Talasiu/Nukuleka & Lapaha Tongan capital, Samoan Pulemelei star mound, Tataga-Matau adzes, and Futuna.

High-precision LA-ICP-MS geochemistry on stone tools from Lapaha reveals long-distance elite adze imports from Tutuila (Tataga-Matau, Samoa), Fiji, and Central Polynesia—integrating fortified Fijian hillfort provinces and Samoan *tiʻa*/Pulemelei chiefly hubs.

guides.title: Aotearoa & Rēkohu: Polynesian Settlement, Pounamu Networks, Pā Fortifications & Wars
guides.description: Rapid ~1280 CE founding settlement, Tūhua obsidian & *pounamu* trade, *pā* hillfort innovation, Musket Wars, New Zealand Wars, and Moriori survival.
guides.intro: Aotearoa New Zealand and Rēkohu (Chatham Islands) were Earth's last major habitable landmasses reached by humans, settling c. 1280–1450 CE through skilled two-way double-hulled canoe voyages.

paragraphs.text: Archaeology at Wairau Bar, Ahuahu, Rakaia, and Raoul Island records an extraordinarily interconnected early phase (c. 1280–1450 CE): Mayor Island obsidian and South Island argillite/pounamu traveled thousands of kilometres across coasts and alpine passes.

By c. 1450–1500 CE, loss of megafauna and sweet-potato intensification coincided with widespread earthwork *pā* hillfort construction, later transformed into anti-cannon trench complexes during the Musket Wars and British-imperial Waikato/Taranaki Wars.

Early 19th-century NSW firearms imports transformed inter-*iwi* warfare before Māori engineers re-designed *pā* trenches to defeat British artillery during the 1845–1872 New Zealand Wars, while isolated Moriori endured the 1835 invasion of Rēkohu.

guides.title: Central & Eastern Polynesia: Taputapuātea, Eiao Adze Trade, Rapa Iti Forts & Rapa Nui
guides.description: Pan-Polynesian ritual voyages at Raʻiatea, 2,400-km Eiao basalt trade, Rapa Iti stone hilltop *pā*, Mangareva–Pitcairn links, and Rapa Nui resilience.
guides.intro: Across an ocean triangle twice the size of Asia, East Polynesian double-hulled voyagers knit distant Societies, Marquesas, Australs, Cooks, Mangareva, Pitcairn, and Rapa Nui into shared sacred and lithic spheres.
guides.scope: Taputapuātea *marae*, Tetiʻaroa atoll imports, Eiao quarry basalt network, Rapa Iti forts, Pitcairn/Mangareva sphere, and Rapa Nui's Anakena/Rano Raraku/*mataʻa* sequence.

map.scope: Unwrapped Central & Eastern Polynesia from Cook and Society Islands (162°W) across Marquesas and Australs to Rapa Nui (109°W).

points.label: Taputapuātea & Tetiʻaroa (Society Islands)
points.description: International *marae* at Opoa paired with atoll sites receiving sourced basalt from Raʻiatea, Tahiti, Eiao, and the Australs.

points.label: Eiao Island Basalt Quarry (Marquesas)
points.description: XRF-sourced fine phonolitic basalt quarry exporting adze blades >2,400 km southwest into the Societies, Tuamotus, and Cooks.

points.label: Rapa Iti Hilltop *Pā* Citadels (Australs)
points.description: Dry-stone summit fortresses crowding central ridges above terraced irrigated taro pondfields.

points.label: Mangareva & Pitcairn Quarry
points.description: Museum and field basalt analyses uniting Pitcairn volcanic glass, Mangareva, and isolated Henderson Island prior to abandonment.

points.label: Rapa Nui (*Rano Raraku* & *Anakena*)
points.description: Monumental *moai* carving, freshwater-anchored *ahu*, rock-mulch gardens, and *mataʻa* re-analysis challenging classic 'ecocide' collapse.

paragraphs.text: Geochemical fingerprinting across Tetiʻaroa, Mangareva, the Cook Islands, and Marquesan quarries proves Central East Polynesians operated deliberate two-way multi-archipelago trade networks between 1000 and 1550 CE before regional isolation.

In isolation across the far southeastern corner, Rapa Iti built densely fortified hilltop *pā* whereas Rapa Nui raised *moai* statues near coastal freshwater lenses and maintained cooperative rock-mulch farms well past 1722 until Peruvian blackbirding raids of 1862–1863.

sections.heading: Rapa Iti stone citadels vs Rapa Nui *moai* landscapes

paragraphs.text: Isolated after ~1500 CE, East Polynesian islands pursued striking political divergence—from densely terraced hilltop *pā* forts crowding remote Rapa Iti to Rapa Nui's ceremonial coastal *ahu* anchored near freshwater lenses.

Modern morphometric studies of stemmed *mataʻa*, stable-isotope diets, and island-wide rock-mulch mapping challenge simple 'ecocide collapse' narratives on Rapa Nui prior to 1860s colonial kidnapping raids.

guides.title: Hawaiʻi: Ahupuaʻa Landscapes, Mauna Kea Quarries, Heiau & Kingdom Unification
guides.description: Alpine basalt workshops at 3,780 m, walled *loko iʻa* fishponds, irrigated taro *loʻi*, monumental *heiau* temples, and Kamehameha I unification.
guides.intro: In the far northern apex of the Polynesian Triangle, Hawaiian *makaʻāinana* and *aliʻi* engineered integrated mountain-to-reef *ahupuaʻa* ecosystems culminating in island-wide kingdoms by the 18th century.
guides.scope: Mauna Kea summit quarry, Kīholo & Oʻahu *loko kuapā* fishponds, Hālawa Valley *heiau* temples, Nānākuli & Molokaʻi quarries, Kahoʻolawe reef sustainability, and 1782–1810 unification.

map.scope: Primary Hawaiian archipelago quarry, aquaculture, temple, and political unification localities.

points.label: Mauna Kea Quarry & Kīholo Fishpond (Hawaiʻi)
points.description: High-altitude summit basalt workshops alongside monumental Kīholo seawalled *loko kuapā* aquaculture.

points.label: Puʻukoholā *Heiau* & Kukuipahu (Kawaihae)
points.description: Cut-and-dressed basalt architecture and Kamehameha I's war-temple dedication in 1791 anchoring unification campaigns.

points.label: Hālawa Valley & Honokoʻi Quarry (Molokaʻi)
points.description: Early coastal dune workshops, basalt quarry production, and ranked valley-to-coast *heiau* temple systems.

points.label: Kahoʻolawe & Leeward Coral Reefs
points.description: Palaeoecological cores documenting sustainable dryland agriculture and eight centuries of managed reef resilience.

points.label: Nānākuli Quarry, Nuʻuanu & Oʻahu Fishponds
points.description: Oʻahu adze quarry distribution, plant microfossils around walled fishponds, and Nuʻuanu Pali's decisive 1795 battle.

paragraphs.text: Above 3,700 metres in alpine cold on Mauna Kea, specialist craftsmen worked the Pacific's largest adze quarry, supplying blades traced by geochemistry alongside Honokoʻi (Molokaʻi) and Nānākuli (Oʻahu) stone tool economies.

Lowland engineers simultaneously constructed walled *loko iʻa* fishponds and expansive leeward sweet-potato field systems while *aliʻi* networks raised massive *heiau* temples leading into Kamehameha I's unification by 1810.

cells: Valley temple hierarchy & basalt quarry reduction
Microfossil fishpond activity & sustainable dryland slopes

sections.heading: *Loko iʻa* fishponds, dryland slopes & reef sustainability

paragraphs.text: Coastal engineering at Kīholo Bay and Oʻahu fishponds combined with extensive leeward colluvial rock-wall agriculture supported centuries of balanced terrestrial and nearshore marine harvesting.

Dressed basalt ritual complexes across Hālawa, Kukuipahu, and Kawaihae trace intensifying *aliʻi* authority leading to Kamehameha I's armed island campaigns and the 1810 unification of the Hawaiian Kingdom.
